title: The `if` statement executes the code inside it only when the condition is True.
when_to_show: When determining which line is executed in an `if` statement
body: An `if` statement executes the indented code inside it only when the result of the conditional expression is `True`.
detail: A comparison expression such as `score >= 60` evaluates to either `True` or `False`, and that result determines the flow of execution. If the condition is `False`, the indented block following the `if` statement is skipped. Therefore, when reading an `if` problem, you must first check the variable values and use those values to determine whether the conditional expression is true or false. When analyzing this concept, rather than simply focusing on getting the correct answer, you should systematically verify which lines set the values and which lines evaluate the conditions or determine the execution path.

title: The `else` clause is the alternative path that is executed when the `if` condition is false.
when_to_show: When choosing which of the two branches of an if/else statement to execute
body: The `else` block is an alternative path that executes when the `if` condition is `False`. If the `if` condition is `True`, the `if` block is executed and the `else` block is skipped.
detail: Conversely, if the `if` condition is `False`, the `if` block is not executed and the `else` block is executed. When reading code, you must not assume that both blocks will be executed. You should interpret the structure as one where only one path is chosen based on the condition’s value. When analyzing this concept, rather than simply focusing on getting the correct answer, you should systematically verify which line determines the value and which line evaluates the condition or position.

title: Comparison operators return True or False.
when_to_show: When reading the meanings of comparison operators such as ==, !=, >, and >=
body: Comparison operators compare two values to return True or False. == checks if the values are equal, and != checks if they are not equal.
detail: >= checks if the value on the left is greater than or equal to the value on the right. Since = is an assignment operator that stores a value, and == is a comparison operator that compares values, it is essential to distinguish between the two. In conditional statements, the result of these comparisons determines whether the code is executed. When reading this concept, rather than just focusing on getting the correct answer, you should check step by step which line sets the value and which line evaluates the condition or position.

title: An empty string and an empty list are treated as "False" in conditional statements.
when_to_show: When reading code that uses values themselves as conditions, such as `if text` or `if items`,
body: A condition evaluates an object's truth value. None, False, numeric zero, empty strings, and empty containers are false; most non-empty containers are true.
detail: A custom object can change the rule with __bool__ or __len__, so do not generalize this as 'anything with a value is true.'

title: List indices start at 0.
when_to_show: When reading code that retrieves values by index, such as `items[0]` and `items[1]`
body: A list index is a way to retrieve values from a list by their position, and in Python, it starts at 0. If `items = ["A", "B", "C"]`, then `items[0]` is "A", `items[1]` is "B", and `items[2]` is "C".
detail: The most important point is that the first value is at index 0, not 1. `len(items)` returns the number of elements in the list. If the length is 3, the valid positive indices are 0, 1, and 2. Therefore, the position of the last element is usually calculated as `len(items) - 1`.

title: append() adds a value to the end of a list
when_to_show: When tracking how the state changes after a value is added to the list
body: `append()` is a method that adds a single value to the end of a list. If you execute `items.append('A')` after `items = []`, `items` becomes `['A']`.
detail: If `append` is called multiple times, the values are appended in the order they were called. When solving output problems, it’s safest to write down the current state of the list each time you encounter an `append` line. When reading this concept, rather than just focusing on getting the correct answer, you should check step by step which lines set values and which lines evaluate conditions or determine positions.

title: len() counts the number of elements in a list
when_to_show: When checking the length of a list after an `append` operation or determining whether a list is empty
body: len() is a function that counts the number of values in a list and returns an integer. The length of an empty list [] is 0, and the length of ["A", "B"] is 2.
detail: len(items) does not print the list itself; instead, it returns the number of elements. Therefore, it is frequently used in comparisons, loops, and conditional expressions. Since lists are mutable, the result of `len` may change if operations such as `append`, `pop`, `remove`, or index assignment are executed beforehand. `append` typically increases the length by 1, while `pop` typically decreases the length by 1.

title: A list allows you to change the value at a specific position.
when_to_show: When reading code that modifies values within a list, such as `items[0] = 'Z'`
body: A list is a mutable data type, meaning its internal values can be changed even after it has been created.
detail: `items[0] = "Z"` does not create a new variable named `items`; instead, it changes the value at index 0 of the list that `items` points to. Therefore, when you print `items` on the next line, you will see the updated value. When reading a list modification problem, you must check both which position has changed and what element was actually at that position. Since indices start at 0, `items[1]` refers to the second value.
